Henry finds pride at the bottom of the quarrel and observes that Ephraim had picked the same fight with Gideon a few chapters earlier, both men being of Manasseh; the two tribes were the nearest of kin, both sons of Joseph, and more jealous of each other than any other pair, since Jacob had crossed his hands and Ephraim would not endure Manasseh receiving honour in the meantime. He calls the anger causeless, since it was the men of Gilead and not of Ephraim who had made Jephthah their captain, so he had no authority to summon them; and outrageous, since men who should have come to congratulate a conqueror and to condole with a bereaved father came instead to burn him in his house. Ellicott gives the tribe the same character from the whole book, slothful and acquiescent under oppression and turbulently arrogant once others have won the victory, and compares them to a Sparta that came late to the field, though Sparta at least congratulated Athens after Marathon. Clarke reads the summons as jealousy lest Gilead should acquire too much power. Gill estimates their number at no fewer than fifty thousand, since forty-two thousand fell.

Jephthah's answer is judged more coolly. Ellicott calls it as moderate as Gideon's without the same happy tact, since it touches on topics that could not but irritate, and adds that we cannot tell whether it was meant conciliatingly; he notes too that the previous appeal to Ephraim is nowhere recorded, which shows how compressed the narrative is. Gill draws out what the answer establishes, that the war had been a contention between the Gileadites and Ammon over territory rather than a private quarrel of Jephthah's, so the two tribes and a half could defend themselves without involving the rest. Clarke traces the phrase about putting his life in his hand to a man laying hold of his weapon, which is at once his sole defence and the thing his enemy will aim at. On the taunt that provoked the slaughter the three part company. Ellicott reads it as a contemptuous disclaimer of kinship, calling the eastern Manassites a race of runaways belonging to neither tribe, and thinks it may have been true enough that debtors and disgraced men fled across the river. Keil reports the sense given by another as a mob of nameless men set between two illustrious tribes. Clarke says plainly that where the point of the reproach lies cannot easily be ascertained.

What the test word meant is disputed, and the dispute matters for how the scene is pictured. Gill takes it for the stream they were standing at, so that the demand was in effect to ask leave to cross, and adds that men in a hurry and off their guard would say it as they always had. Keil agrees it is a stream or flood and rejects the alternative outright, holding that an ear of corn is quite unsuitable here; Ellicott reports both, giving ford, depth of waters and channel from the Hebrew but noting that the Greek version rendered it an ear of corn, and that one manuscript simply paraphrases it as the watchword. Clarke spends his space on whether the two letters could really be told apart, arguing against those who find the difference imperceptible that a Hebrew ear caught it at once, as an Arabic speaker distinguishes two letters a European never hears, and that the spelling itself proves it, since the other letter would not have been used if there were nothing to mark. Ellicott draws the moral the word has since acquired, that it stands for the minute differences religious parties press to ferocity, and is careful to say that here the pronunciation was not the reason for killing a man but only the sign that he was an Ephraimite.

Gill accounts for the shortness of Jephthah's six years by supposing him depressed and worn away with grief over his daughter and his other troubles. Ellicott observes how little the title tells us, since nothing in the book shows what the limits of a judge's jurisdiction were or how much authority the office carried, and Keil supplies what can be inferred, that the formula marks these men as successors of Jephthah one after another and so confines their rule to the tribes east of Jordan and perhaps the northern ones west of it. On the burial Ellicott presses a textual point. The Hebrew says only in cities of Gilead, which might mean in one of them, but the grave of so renowned a man was not likely to be forgotten, and a single altered letter gives the reading of the Greek and Latin versions, in his own city, Gilead. Henry sets the whole run of brief judgeships under a proverb, that for the transgression of a land many are its princes, good men being removed just as their usefulness begins.

Which Bethlehem produced Ibzan splits the commentators two against two. Henry takes it for Bethlehem of Judah, David's city, and draws the consequence he wants, that the town was of old famous for increase and was the very place where he should be born whose spiritual seed would be as the stars. Gill reports Josephus to the same effect and adds the rabbinic identification of Ibzan with Boaz, on the ground that Boaz was of that town and lived in the days of the judges. Ellicott rejects both. He says the notion that Ibzan is Boaz has nothing whatever to support it, and gives two reasons against Judah, that this book itself distinguishes the southern town as Bethlehem Judah, and that Judah at this period seems to have stood aloof from the general life of the nation; since there was a Bethlehem in Zebulun and the next judge was a Zebulonite, he prefers that. Keil agrees, saying it is hardly the town in Judah despite Josephus. On the sixty children Gill notes how uncommon an equal division of the sexes is, and sets the contrast with Jephthah, who had one daughter and she unmarriageable by his vow.

For the last two judges Ellicott works almost entirely on names. Elon means a terebinth, and he remarks that easterners are still named from trees, one of his own muleteers in Palestine having been called father of olives; the place of that judge's burial is the same word with different vowels and means a gazelle rather than a terebinth. Abdon means servant, and the name of his father is the first appearance of one afterwards famous in Jewish learning. He also corrects the English of the next verse, since the Hebrew says sons of sons and the older usage of nephews always meant grandsons. Keil fills in the ground instead, locating one burial place in ruins some hours east of Akka and the other in a village south-west of Nablus which was also the home of one of David's heroes. On the seventy ass colts Ellicott takes the trappings as a mark of wealth and command, and Clarke translates the custom into his own terms, that riding fine asses then was no less dignified than riding in coaches now, so that the family all kept their carriages. Clarke also adds up the thirty-one years of quiet these judgeships covered, notes that nothing is recorded of their administration or of the state of religion under them, and concludes that God was doubtless at work with none to record it.
